newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine property market seen hit by high rates.
newsitem.headline: Philippine property market seen hit by high rates.

text.p: First-half results from Philippine property firms show profit growth slowing from last year's dizzying heights and analysts on Wednesday said high interest rates should keep the sector under pressure.

"We do not expect bulls. But we do not expect busts either. Property is still growing but because of aberrations in the cost of money, there would be flat growth in demand to be expected in the second half," said Helen Alvarez, research director at Asia Capital and Trust Corp.

Several property firms in recent weeks reported slower earnings growth in the first six months of the year, weighed down by fears of a property glut, especially in the high-end residential and office sectors.

Of eight property firms that have reported interim results so far, earnings have grown on average by 25 percent, said Raul Ruiz, research director of Sun Hung Kai Securities. That compares with spectacular annual earnings growth of 91 percent for 1996.

"Earnings growth cannot be the same as last year," he said. But he added that profits had generally been in line with expectations and he was forecasting annual 1997 earnings growth of 29 percent for the sector.

Property has been under the spotlight in the Philippines, mostly due to fears that the market could shadow problems now plaguing its financially troubled Southeast Asian neighbour -- Thailand, whose overheated property sector led to an economic crisis.

Although government officials in Manila and several analysts have maintained the Philippines was a healthy investment destination, property market fears have battered Manila stocks, knocking the overall market to two-year lows in April.

Since then, Philippine shares have drifted lower as investors focus on high commercial interest rates -- currently hovering at two-year highs of 18 percent after reaching 32 percent last month -- and weakness in the local peso following a de facto devaluation on July 11.

The devaluation, which has wiped away about 10 percent of the peso's value, was effectively forced on to the Philippines by currency speculators following a similar de facto devaluation in the Thai baht on July 2.
Although some investors linked the Philippines with Thailand, recent results show earnings in the Philippine property market cooling down.

Megaworld Properties and Holdings Inc recently reported a lower-than-expected four percent rise in first-half net income to 842.5 million pesos ($29.1 million), while its unit Empire East Land Holdings Inc also posted lacklustre earnings with a nine percent rise to 723.8 million pesos.
Leading property firm Ayala Land Inc reported just five percent growth in net profit to 2.66 billion pesos compared to 52 percent growth last year.
Filinvest Land Inc outshined its peers and managed to do well despite the current environment, posting 46 percent growth in first half net to 822.6 million pesos.

Some analysts said the sector could suffer further weakness after the central bank in late April imposed a 30 percent limit on loans by banks to property firms and banks became stricter in their lending after Thailand's financial woes.
"The property sector has always been cyclical. It would take six months to one year at least to recover," said Wilfred Son Keng Po, managing director of Angping & Associates Securities Inc.
He said uncertainty on the political front with no clear front-runner to next year's presidential elections could also weigh on the sector.
"Uncertainty doesn't augur well for the economy, ergo also for the property sector," Son Keng Po said.
